title: How to work a half cross-stitch
subtitle: The single diagonal used for backgrounds and shading
excerpt: A half cross-stitch is the first diagonal of a full cross-stitch worked alone. It covers less fabric than a full cross, which makes it useful for pale background areas, shadow shading at the edges of a motif, and any section where a lighter texture is called for.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, needlework chapter.

glossaryTerms.definition: Only the first diagonal of a full cross-stitch. The stitch runs from bottom-left to top-right over one Aida square. It produces lighter coverage than a full cross and is used for pale backgrounds, shading, or areas where the chart calls for a less solid fill.

worked alone. It runs bottom-left to top-right over one Aida square and sits at roughly half the visual weight of a full cross. Charts use it for background areas that should read as pale or airy, or to suggest a shadow on the edge of a motif.

The stitch leaves gaps in the fabric coverage. On fine Aida counts the fabric weave shows through between the diagonal threads. This is the intended effect; a half cross-stitch background reads as lighter than the filled areas around it, creating depth in the finished piece.
Come up at the bottom-left hole.
Bring the needle up at the bottom-left corner of the Aida square.
Go down at the top-right hole.
Push the needle down at the top-right corner of the same square. One diagonal is on the fabric. Stop here: this is the half cross-stitch. Do not come back with the second diagonal.
When filling a background area, work all the half cross-stitches across the row in one direction before moving to the next row. All diagonals must lean the same way across the whole section.

Cross-stitch charts mark half-stitches with a single diagonal line inside the square rather than a full X. Read the chart key before starting: some charts use the half-stitch to indicate shading where a full cross would be too dense, while others use it to suggest the very edge of a curved shape.

The three-quarter cross-stitch pairs with the quarter cross-stitch to share a single Aida square between two colours. Together they produce curved outlines and rounded shapes that a full-square grid cannot otherwise achieve.
